newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chips drop on fears of higher interest rates. [Corrected 00:56 gmt 12/12]
newsitem.headline: Blue-chips drop on fears of higher interest rates. [Corrected 00:56 gmt 12/12]

text.p: Blue-chip stocks dropped sharply Wednesday, shaken by a sell-off in bonds amid fears that interest rates might be headed higher and worries about corporate earnings.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 70.73 points, or 1.09 percent, at 6,402.52 after trading briefly with a loss of nearly 130 points.

Just last Friday, the index slumped 145 points before recovering to end down 55 points on cautionary comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets.
In the broader market, declining issues swamped advances 2,122 to 506 on active volume of 494 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
While the blue-chip market dropped, the Nasdaq Composite index shed only 3.43 to 1,309.12 as bellwether Intel Corp. rallied 7-3/4 to 136-7/8.
"The tape looked bad this morning, like the world was coming to an end," said James Cramer, president of Cramer Co.
The stock market got off to a bad start as bonds suffered a meltdown on speculation that Japanese investors might be losing their appetite for U.S. Treasury securities.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell (corrects from "rose") more than 1-3/4 points, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, shot up to 6.63 percent -- its highest since the close of business on Nov. 6 -- vs. 6.49 percent Tuesday.
The recent strength in bond prices had helped fuel the rally in stocks, with the long-term yield slipping below the psychologically important 6.50 percent.
"The bond market has stopped going lower in terms of yields and that's important for the stock market," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal & Co.
The sustained jump in long-term yields could make bonds more attractive than stocks to investors.
The bond market sell-off was sparked by comments from Robert Hormats, a vice chairman at Goldman Sachs International.

In an interview broadcast on Reuters Financial Television, Hormats said he thought the rising U.S. trade imbalance posed a potential threat to dollar-based assets, which in turn could quell Japanese institutional investors' thirst for U.S. Treasury bonds.

Japan's trade surplus with the United States soared 31.3 percent in October to $3.13 billion, according to Japan's Finance Ministry. The huge Japanese trade surpluses with the United States, have been a source of friction.
In late trading Wednesday, the dollar fell to 112.92 Japanese yen from 113.40 yen on Tuesday.

Wall Street was greeted by tame wholesale inflation data, with November producer prices up 0.4 percent as energy prices posted the biggest jump since April. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the core rate rose 0.1 percent.
Among the winners, Intel surged after Merrill Lynch analyst Thomas Kurlak raised his 1997 earnings estimate on the computer chip giant.

An Intel manufacturing executive told a Montgomery Securities conference in San Francisco that the company's chipmaking factories were at full production, a sign of strong demand for computers and other high-tech gear.
IBM fell 1-7/8 to 156-1/8. The company declined comment on market rumours that it was about to issue a profit warning and said it planned no press releases on Wednesday.
Alexander & Alexander Services rose 3 to 17-1/8 and AON Corp. added 1-1/4 to 58-7/8. AON agreed to acquire Alexander & Alexander for $17.50 per common share.
MoneyGram Payment Systems Inc., a non-bank provider of consumer money wire transfer services, surged 1-5/8 to 13-5/8 in its first day of trading.
Another inital public offering, Skymall Inc., an in-flight catalogue company that sells merchandise to airline passengers, rose 3/4 to 8-3/4.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 6.81 to 740.73. The American Stock Exchange index lost 6.87 to 583.92.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 4.36 to 389.54. The average share was down 45 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,177.886 down 72.431 or 1.00 percent.
